issue.issue_text: Whether a claim of juvenility can be made after the judgment of conviction and sentence has attained finality?

facts: The applicant was convicted by the Supreme Court and was serving his sentence.
After the judgment of conviction and sentence became final, the applicant filed a miscellaneous application.
In this application, he claimed for the first time that he was a juvenile (under 18 years old) on the date the offense was committed.
The State argued against this, stating that the claim was highly belated and should be dismissed because it was made long after the conviction was finalized.
law: The Court relied on its own precedent, specifically the judgments in 'Abuzar Hossain vs. State of West Bengal' and 'Pramila vs. State of Chhattisgarh'.
These precedents establish the legal principle that a claim of juvenility can be made at any stage of criminal proceedings, even after the judgment of conviction and sentence has become final.
application: Applying the established legal principle, the Court rejected the State's argument that the claim was too late.
The Court affirmed that the finality of the conviction did not bar the applicant from raising the plea of juvenility.
To verify the claim, the Court directed a Sessions Judge to conduct an inquiry into the applicant's age.

The Sessions Judge submitted a report, based on evidence and documents as per Section 94 of the Juvenile Justice Act 2015, which confirmed that the applicant was indeed a juvenile on the date of the incident.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a claim of juvenility can be made even after a judgment of conviction and sentence has attained finality. Based on this principle and the findings of the inquiry report which proved the applicant was a juvenile, the Court accepted the claim, set aside his conviction, and acquitted him.

issue.issue_text: Whether the applicant was a juvenile on the date of the commission of the offence?

facts: The applicant was convicted by the Supreme Court for an offence committed on 17.01.2002.
After conviction, the applicant filed an application claiming he was a juvenile at the time of the offence.
The Supreme Court directed the Sessions Court to conduct an enquiry into the applicant's age.
The Sessions Judge conducted a detailed enquiry, examining the applicant, his mother, and a school official, and submitted a report.
The report concluded that the applicant's date of birth is 04.10.1984, making him 17 years, 3 months, and 13 days old on the date of the offence.
law: Under the precedent set in cases like Abuzar Hossain vs. State of West Bengal and Pramila vs. State of Chhattisgarh, a claim of juvenility can be made at any stage, even after a conviction has become final.
Section 94 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 provides the framework for the determination of age.
application: The Court first established that it was permissible to hear the juvenility claim despite it being filed after the conviction had attained finality, based on established legal precedent.
The Court relied on the factual findings of the report submitted by the Sessions Judge, which was prepared after a detailed enquiry as per the Court's direction.
The Court accepted the Sessions Judge's conclusion that the applicant's date of birth was proven to be 04.10.1984.
Based on this date of birth, the Court calculated that the applicant was under eighteen years of age on 17.01.2002, the date the offence was committed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the report of the Sessions Judge, upheld the applicant's claim of juvenility, set aside his conviction, and acquitted him.

appellant_arguments: The applicant, citing the judgment in Abuzar Hossain vs. State of West Bengal, contended that a claim for juvenility can be made at any stage of the criminal proceedings, even after the final conviction and sentence have been imposed.

appellant_arguments: The applicant argued that a comprehensive enquiry, which examined the applicant, his mother, and the school headmaster, had been conducted and its report should be accepted.
The applicant contended that a slight discrepancy in his name between prosecution records and school records should not negate his claim, as his identity as the son of Ramji Lal was not in dispute.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: No binding legal rule is present in the provided text. The text only contains factual background, procedural history, and the final decision of the court in this specific miscellaneous application.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court concluded that a claim of juvenility can be raised at any stage, even after a conviction has attained finality. Based on an enquiry report by the Sessions Judge, which it accepted as the State had failed to challenge the evidence during the enquiry, the Court found that the applicant was a juvenile on the date of the offense. Consequently, the Court set aside his conviction and acquitted him.
legal_tests_applied: The principle established in precedents, specifically Pramila vs. State of Chhattisgarh, that "an application for claiming juvenility may be made even after the judgment and order of conviction and sentence has been granted against a person which has attained finality."
Section 94 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, which was the basis for the Sessions Judge's enquiry and determination of the applicant's age.
why_respondent_won: The applicant's claim was accepted because the Court followed its own precedent (Pramila vs. State of Chhattisgarh), which explicitly permits a claim of juvenility to be made even after a conviction and sentence have become final.

The Court accepted the factual finding of the Sessions Judge's enquiry that the applicant was a juvenile, as this finding was based on an examination of witnesses and documents in accordance with Section 94 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015.

The State's objection to the enquiry report was dismissed because the State had failed to cross-examine any of the witnesses (the applicant, his mother, and the headmaster) during the enquiry, thereby forfeiting its right to challenge the report's conclusions.
policy_considerations: The decision upholds the fundamental policy of the Juvenile Justice Act, which is to ensure that an individual who was a child at the time of an offense is not subjected to the rigors and consequences of the adult criminal justice system, irrespective of when the definitive proof of age is brought before the court.
